stem: On the labelled West Africa outline, connect the Saharan salt sources to the gold-producing areas south of them. Explain why traders travelled between them.
answer: Routes cross different resource zones; each side gets a scarce good. Ancient Ghana lay inland, north of the modern country.
steps: salt in the Sahara and gold to the south both placed | exchange of scarce goods explained | ancient Ghana placed inland, not on the modern coast
samples: Salt came from mines in the desert and gold from the lands near the upper rivers; each side lacked what the other had, so traders crossed. | Ghana is on the coast, so the gold came from there.

stem: Locate Axum near the Red Sea and the Swahili towns along the Indian Ocean coast. Which kingdom is earlier? Give one benefit of a port.
answer: Axum is earlier; ports connect inland producers with sea traders.
steps: Axum by the Red Sea and Swahili towns on the East African coast | Axum named as earlier | one benefit of a port
samples: Axum, by the Red Sea, is centuries earlier; Kilwa and Mombasa are on the Indian Ocean. A port lets inland goods reach ships. | Axum and the Swahili towns were one empire at the same time.

stem: On the Central Asia map, choose the oasis route or the shorter waterless route for a caravan. Explain your choice, and say whether one merchant must carry the goods from China to Europe.
answer: Water and stopping places support the oasis route; goods pass through many merchants.
steps: oasis route chosen for water and stopping places | goods pass from merchant to merchant
samples: The oasis route is longer but has water and markets to rest and trade at; goods change hands many times. | One merchant took the silk all the way to Europe.

stem: Invented for practice: House R inherits rule and governs several peoples. Apply the words dynasty and empire to House R, and explain why both can fit.
answer: Dynasty names the ruling family that passes rule down; empire names its rule over several peoples; both describe House R at once.
steps: dynasty tied to the ruling family | empire tied to rule over several peoples | explains that both fit at once
samples: House R is a dynasty because rule passes within one family, and an empire because it rules several peoples; the words name different things. | House R is a dynasty, so it cannot be an empire.

stem: On the new resource inset, link two producing zones and a market. Explain who could tax the exchange and who was forced into it.
answer: Rulers could tax routes and markets; enslaved people were traded by force or made to labour.
steps: two zones and a market linked | rulers taxing routes or markets named | enslaved people named as people forced, not as goods
samples: Gold from the south and salt from the north met at the market town, where the king's officials could take a share. Enslaved people were forced across the desert or made to dig. | The trade made everyone rich.

stem: Invented for practice: a Timbuktu manuscript copied in 1700 names a royal patron. Explain one way trade, power and learning could be linked, and why this manuscript alone cannot show what Mansa Musa read.
answer: Trade wealth can support patrons and scholars; a later copy cannot alone show an earlier ruler's reading.
steps: a link among trade, rulers and scholars | the late date named as a limit | copying and keeping by families or scholars named
samples: Trade brought wealth that let rulers and families pay for scholars and books, but a copy made long after Musa died cannot show what he read. | The manuscript shows what Musa read.

stem: On the unused inset, link Great Zimbabwe's interior to Kilwa and an overseas market. Does an imported object found at a town prove that foreign people built it? Explain.
answer: Relays carry inland gold to the coast and across the sea; an imported object shows exchange, not foreign builders.
steps: interior, coast and overseas market linked in order | imported objects read as exchange | the builders named as local
samples: Gold went from the interior to Kilwa and over the sea, and goods came back; a bowl from abroad shows trade, while the walls were built by the people who lived there. | Bowls from abroad were found there, so foreigners built it.

stem: Invented for practice: two historians' captions cite the same interview. How many independent witnesses have they shown, and which inference needs checking?
answer: One witness, not two; each caption's inference is checked against the interview itself.
steps: one witness named | the inference to check named | checked against the underlying interview
samples: Both captions rest on one interview, so there is one witness; I would check whether the interview says what the second caption claims. | Two captions, so two witnesses.

stem: Invented for practice: two histories cite one court report, and a folded third card lists a market tax. Write a question about who gained, open the third card, and answer from it.
answer: The shared report is one witness; the tax card adds rulers' receipts but not workers' views.
steps: a question about who gained | the third card opened and a detail used | what is still unknown named
samples: Who gained from the market? The tax card shows the ruler took a share of each sale, but not what the sellers thought of it. | I would look up the tax records.

stem: Invented for practice: a caption calls the Mongol conquest a peaceful opening of markets. Correct the caption, and explain why a chronicler's exact count of the dead needs checking.
answer: Name the killing, destruction and forced rule; a chronicler's number depends on his access and needs other sources.
steps: killing and destruction named plainly | trade gains kept apart from harms | the count checked for access and corroboration
samples: The conquest killed many people and destroyed cities before trade grew; a chronicler who was not there needs other sources for his number. | The conquest was worth it because trade grew.

stem: On the new two-region inset, add one good moving each way and explain why caravans stopped at the marked place.
answer: One supported good each way, with water, supplies or a market explaining the stop.
steps: a good each way | each good tied to where it came from | the stop explained by water, supplies or exchange
samples: Horses go one way and silk the other; caravans stop at the oasis for water and to trade. | Silk went west, and nothing came back.

stem: Invented for practice: a caption places Zheng He's voyages under Yuan rule. Correct it, and explain what the voyages could add to knowledge of the world.
answer: The voyages came under the early Ming, after Yuan rule ended; records of ports and routes added knowledge, with limits.
steps: Ming, not Yuan | after the Yuan named in order | one addition to knowledge, with a limit
samples: Zheng He sailed for the Ming, after the Yuan fell; records of ports and routes told readers in China about lands across the Indian Ocean, from the court's point of view. | Zheng He sailed for Khubilai Khan.

stem: Compare the unused Rabban Sauma passage with the unused Marco Polo passage. What could each man know, and how could readers learn about lands beyond their own region?
answer: A diplomat and a merchant had different access; who wrote the account down, and for whom, limits what readers learn.
steps: what each could see, from his journey | how the account reached readers | one limit
samples: Rabban Sauma met kings as an envoy; Polo served the Khan and traded; readers learned of distant courts and routes, through scribes who may have added things. | Polo saw everything in his book himself.

stem: Invented for practice: a court label praises a ruler's inherited authority over several peoples as proof that everyone supported him. Apply two words for power, and judge the claim of support.
answer: Dynasty and empire can both fit; praise from the court does not prove subjects' consent.
steps: two words for power applied | the words allowed to overlap | the court label judged as self-presentation
samples: He is from a dynasty and rules an empire; the court wrote the label, so it shows how he wanted to be seen, not what his subjects thought. | The label shows his people agreed to his rule.

stem: Invented for practice: a ruler taxes a river crossing that inland farmers and miners supply. Mark the connection on the map, and explain what it meant for the ruler's power and for the economy.
answer: The crossing tied the ruler's revenue and authority to the producers' labour and to exchange.
steps: connection marked from producers to crossing to market | political meaning: revenue and control | economic meaning: whose labour and which goods
samples: Farmers and miners send goods to the crossing, where the ruler's officials take a share; the tax pays for his soldiers, and the goods come from other people's work. | The ruler was rich because the river was there.

stem: Invented for practice: state R lasts from 1180 to 1360 and state S from 1270 to 1420, and imported ceramics turn up at R's port. Plot both on a timeline, give the overlap, and explain one link to another region without claiming foreign founders.
answer: Overlap 1270 to 1360; the ceramics show exchange with another region, not foreign builders.
steps: two separate dated bands | overlap given | the ceramics read as exchange, not founders
samples: R and S overlap from 1270 to 1360; the ceramics show R's port traded with another region, but local people built the port. | The ceramics show foreigners founded R.

stem: Invented for practice: a trading town grows wealthy under its ruler while a local record lists forced labour. Which detail challenges the claim that trade benefited everyone, and how?
answer: The forced labour shows a cost carried by people who did not share the wealth.
steps: the forced-labour detail chosen | who carried the cost named | the claim judged, not repeated
samples: The forced labour: the town got rich from work people were made to do, so not everyone benefited. | The town was rich, so everyone gained.

stem: Choose one assessment component marked 1 or 0 and correct it alone. Then put one development from this unit beside one from another region on the parallel timeline, and explain why they belong side by side.
answer: A missed component corrected with evidence; two developments placed in the same years and the overlap explained.
steps: the missed component corrected with evidence | two developments placed in the same years | the overlap explained
samples: I corrected A2b: Axum was earlier, and the Swahili towns had their own rulers. Mali under Mansa Musa and the Yuan under Khubilai's successors both ruled in the early 1300s. | Mali rose after the Mongol Empire fell.

stem: Sort three statements about a ruler of Mali into what a court source shows and what it cannot show about his subjects' support.
answer: Ceremony, wealth and titles are shown; subjects' consent is not.
steps: each statement sorted | the reason for each given
samples: The gold cap shows wealth; the guards show force; neither shows what farmers thought. | The ceremony shows everyone loved him.

stem: Invented for practice: at a mountain-pass market a king's deputy takes a share of every load of copper. Turn the case into a map label and a two-sentence explanation of its politics and its economy.
answer: Label: the pass, the market and the deputy, dated. Politics: the deputy collects for the king. Economy: miners and carriers produce what is taxed.
steps: a dated label at the right place | politics: who collects and for whom | economy: who works and which good
samples: Pass market (invented case): the king's deputy takes copper from each load, so the pass pays for royal power; the copper comes from miners and carriers, not the king. | The king was rich because of the mountains.

stem: Map-and-explain product, part 1: draw a dated map of your option with a key, a scale and its routes, then explain its politics and its economy from two named sources.
answer: A dated map with key, scale and routes; politics and economy each explained from a named source, labour and costs included.
steps: dated map: years in the title, key, scale | centres and routes placed | politics explained from a named source | economy explained from a named source, with who worked and who gained | evidence kept apart from inference
samples: Mali about 1330: Niani, Timbuktu and Walata on the Niger and the desert routes; the court source shows a ruler with armed guards and gold, and traders brought salt and beads to buy food and gold. | Mali was a big rich empire, shown with today's borders.

stem: Add one producer and one cost to an arrow on yesterday's exit map.
answer: A named producer and a named cost on the arrow.
steps: a producer named | a cost named
samples: Miners dig the gold; carriers walk it to the crossing and pay the toll. | The arrow shows trade.

stem: Map-and-explain product, part 2: add your option's culture and every link to other regions (trade, alliance, war, exchange) to your map, with a source for each link or a note that no source on your sheet records it.
answer: Culture and each of the four links shown, each with a source or an honest note.
steps: culture explained with a named contributor beyond the ruler | trade link with a source | alliance link with a source, or a note that none is recorded | war link with a source | exchange of ideas or people with a source
samples: Kilwa: mosques and the sultan's alms show Islam in town life; gold came up the coast from Sufala; the sultan raided inland (war); no source on my sheet names an alliance. | The Swahili towns were Arab colonies, and that is their culture.

stem: Add Mali and the Yuan dynasty to the class parallel timeline as two separate bands, and mark the years they overlap.
answer: Two separate bands; the overlap marked.
steps: two separate bands | the overlap marked
samples: Mali from about 1235 and the Yuan from 1271 to 1368; they overlap in the 1300s. | Mali and the Yuan were the same empire.

stem: Read the written feedback on your map. Copy the label or sentence it questions, and name the evidence it asks for.
answer: The questioned label copied and the evidence named.
steps: the questioned label copied | the evidence named
samples: Feedback asks where my alliance came from; I need a source or a note that none is recorded. | The feedback says good job.

stem: Revise your map and explanation from the feedback. Change the content the feedback questions, not only the words, and keep the first version.
answer: A revised map and explanation that answer the feedback, first version kept.
steps: each questioned point changed in substance | evidence added or the claim narrowed | first version kept
samples: I removed the border I could not date and added the Polo source for paper money under economy. | I made the map neater.

stem: In the discussion, give one detail from a source for trade, faith or the sword, and answer a classmate's detail with a detail from another source.
answer: A sourced detail and a sourced reply.
steps: a detail with its source named | a reply from another source
samples: Polo says no one dared refuse the paper money on pain of death, so trade there rested on the sword. | Trade, because they were rich.

stem: Closing claim: was a ruler's power in this age won mainly by trade, by faith or by the sword? Answer for one African ruler and for the Mongol rulers. Explain two details from the sources, answer one counterclaim and name one limit of the sources. Include how rule changed from Chinggis Khan to Khubilai Khan and one consequence for the Silk Roads.
answer: A claim weighing trade, faith and the sword, two explained details, an answered counterclaim and a named limit; the change from Chinggis to Khubilai and a Silk Roads consequence.
steps: claim weighs the three, not one alone | two details explained from named sources | a counterclaim answered with evidence | a limit of the sources named | Chinggis to Khubilai: conquest to Yuan government | a Silk Roads consequence, with conquest's harms kept
samples: The sword came first for the Mongols: Ibn al-Athir describes whole cities killed; under Khubilai the Yuan ruled through government and paper money that Polo says no one dared refuse, which helped merchants on the roads. In Mali, faith and trade worked together: Ibn Battuta saw crowded mosques and salt and beads traded for food. Counterclaim: Mali's ruler also had armed guards. Limit: both writers were outsiders. | Trade, because both were rich.

stem: Revise your closing claim from the written feedback. Change what the feedback questions, keep the first version, and note what you changed.
answer: The questioned part changed in substance and a short note.
steps: the questioned part changed | a note on what changed
samples: I added the Yuan date and kept the killing beside the trade. | I fixed spelling.

stem: With your response group, redo the assessment component your group missed, using the move the teacher gives.
answer: The component redone with the repair move.
steps: the move used | the component answered again
samples: Our group redid A3: silk west, horses east, furs south. | We copied the key.

stem: Review units 1 to 3 on the parallel timeline: name two developments that happened at the same time in different regions, and one network that linked regions.
answer: Two simultaneous developments in different regions and one network.
steps: two developments in the same years | different regions | a network named
samples: Mali and the Yuan ruled at the same time; the Indian Ocean routes linked Kilwa to Asia. | Rome and Mali were at the same time.

stem: Invented for practice: House T passes rule to its children and governs several peoples; Lord U grants land in return for military service. Define the three words for power printed on your paper, apply one to House T or Lord U, and explain why another word also fits.
answer: Hereditary rule: rule passed by descent. Dynasty: a ruling family. Kingdom: a realm under a monarch. Empire: rule over several peoples or lands. Feudal society: land given for service. The words overlap and help compare power.
steps: three words defined accurately | one applied to the case | a second word shown to fit too | why the words help compare power
samples: House T's rule is hereditary and dynastic; its rule over several peoples makes it an empire. Lord U's land for service is feudal, a different relationship, so the words help compare kinds of power. | An empire cannot have a dynasty.

stem: Map-and-explain product, revised after written feedback: a dated map of Ghana, Mali and Songhai, of the Swahili city-states with earlier Axum, or of the Mongol Empire, with key, scale and routes; its politics, economy and culture; and its links to other regions by trade, alliance, war and exchange, each from a named source.
answer: Scored by component: map, politics, economy, culture, trade, alliance, war, exchange, two named sources, evidence kept apart from inference.
steps: map: dated, key, scale, routes | politics from a source | economy with labour and costs | culture with contributors beyond the ruler | trade | alliance, or a note that none is recorded | war | exchange | two named sources | evidence kept apart from inference
samples: Mali: Niger towns and desert routes tied taxes and royal authority to trade; mosques and scholars show learned networks; a traveller's court account cannot show every subject's consent. | Mali was rich, so everyone supported its king.

stem: Place Ghana, Mali and Songhai in order. Explain how gold, salt and the trade in enslaved people supported their power, and how Timbuktu connected trade and learning.
answer: Three separate, partly overlapping states in order; rulers taxed and controlled exchange, including people forced into slavery; trade wealth supported scholars in Timbuktu.
steps: Ghana, Mali, Songhai in order | gold and salt exchange taxed or controlled | enslaved people named as people forced | Timbuktu linking trade and learning
samples: Ghana, then Mali, then Songhai led at different times; rulers taxed the gold and salt trade, and enslaved people were forced across the desert; trade paid for books and scholars in Timbuktu. | They were one state that traded only gold.

stem: On the unused inset, locate earlier Axum and the medieval Swahili coast. Explain one political and one economic contrast between them.
answer: Axum: an earlier Red Sea kingdom under one king. Swahili towns: later, separately governed city-states trading on the Indian Ocean.
steps: Axum placed earlier, by the Red Sea | Swahili towns placed later, on the Indian Ocean coast | a political contrast | an economic contrast
samples: Axum was one earlier kingdom on the Red Sea; the later Swahili towns each had their own ruler and traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean. | Axum ruled every Swahili town.

stem: Explain one contact between the Mongol Empire and Europeans, one achievement of Yuan rule and one achievement of the early Ming. The change from Chinggis Khan to Khubilai Khan and a Silk Roads consequence are scored from your revised closing claim.
answer: A named contact (Polo, Rubruck or Rabban Sauma); a Yuan achievement such as paper money across the realm or theatre; early Ming voyages of Zheng He after 1368.
steps: European contact named and explained | a Yuan achievement | an early Ming achievement, after the Yuan | from the claim: Chinggis to Khubilai and a Silk Roads consequence
samples: Rubruck reached Mongke Khan as a Christian envoy; the Yuan made paper money pass across the realm; the early Ming sent Zheng He across the Indian Ocean. | Zheng He sailed for Chinggis Khan.

stem: On the unused route map, label silk, horses, grain, furs and spices from the new goods cards, each with where it came from and which way it moved. Explain how the network linked Europe, Africa and Asia without every good crossing all three.
answer: Silk west from China; horses from the steppe to China and other markets; furs south from northern forests; spices west from South and Southeast Asia; grain among nearby towns; relays link the regions.
steps: five goods each with origin and direction | goods moving in several directions | relays or regional exchange explained | grain as regional
samples: Silk moves west, horses toward China, furs south and spices west and north through connected markets; grain feeds nearby towns. No single caravan carries everything. | Everything went west from China.

stem: Read P1 and P2. Explain what the travel account and the atlas each added to knowledge of the world, who might use each, and one limit of each.
answer: P1 adds salt mining by enslaved people, provisions brought from far off and salt used as money; P2 tells distant European readers that Mali's ruler had gold. P1 was dictated years later; P2's maker worked from reports, not a visit.
steps: what P1 added | what P2 added | a user of each | a limit of each tied to how it was made
samples: P1 tells readers how salt was dug, by whom and what it was worth; P2 told European readers Mali was rich in gold. P1 was dictated after the journey; P2's maker never went to Mali. | The atlas proves its maker visited Mali.

stem: Trace each half of statement S to P1 or P2. Explain one inference S makes from the sources and one claim the sources cannot support.
answer: Provisions brought from far off support the connection claim; the gold image supports a reputation; equal benefit or exact borders are not supported.
steps: first half traced to P1 | second half traced to P2 | one inference explained | one unsupported claim named
samples: Food brought to Taghaza from elsewhere supports the first half; the atlas figure with gold supports the second. Neither shows who received the wealth. | S is true because a historian wrote it.

stem: Write a question that P1 and P2 raise together. Choose F1 or F2 and say why, open it, and record a detail that answers or changes your question. Name what is still unresolved.
answer: A question from both sources, a reasoned choice, a detail from the card actually read, and what is left open.
steps: a question that needs both sources | a reasoned choice of card | a detail from the card | the question revised or answered | what is still unresolved
samples: Who controlled the trade? I chose F1 because it is about a trading town: the sultan's deputy met merchants with armed guards. It still does not tell me what the miners thought. | I would search for more facts.
